Resting meat.title: Resting meat
Resting meat.sub: Why you wait before you cut
Resting meat.explain: Let's say you pull a steak off the pan and cut it right away. The juice runs out over the board, and what's left on your plate is dry. Heat pushes the juice toward the middle of the meat. Give it a few minutes off the heat and it settles back through the whole piece. Same steak, nothing lost to the board. The waiting is part of the cooking.
Resting meat.action: Take it off the heat, put it on a warm plate, cover it loosely. Five minutes for a steak, fifteen for a roast. Then cut.

The bloom.title: The bloom
The bloom.sub: The first pour, and why it is small
The bloom.explain: Let's say your coffee keeps coming out thin and sour, and you've already tried grinding finer. Fresh grounds are full of gas, and gas pushes water away, so most of your pour runs past the coffee. Wet them with a splash first, twice the weight of the coffee, and wait. The bed puffs into a dome and the bubbles stop. Now the water can get in. Thirty seconds, and the rest of the pour finally works.
The bloom.action: Pour twice the coffee's weight in water, just enough to wet everything. Wait thirty seconds. Then pour the rest.

Companion planting.title: Companion planting
Companion planting.sub: Who you put next to what
Companion planting.explain: Let's say something keeps eating your tomatoes and you'd rather not spray. A bed with one crop in it is an easy meal. Put basil around the base and marigolds at the end of the row. The smell confuses what's hunting, and the marigolds pull pests toward the flowers. You keep the tomatoes. Some plants are just easier to grow next to each other.
Companion planting.action: Plant basil at the base of each tomato and marigolds at both ends of the bed. Keep the basil close, about a hand's width out.

Packing cubes.title: Packing cubes
Packing cubes.explain: Let's say you're moving hotels every second night. By day three the case is a pile, and finding one clean shirt means taking everything out and putting it back. Cubes fix the sorting, not the space. One for shirts, one for layers, one for socks, one for the dirty stuff. You decide where things live once, at home. You stop unpacking. You just lift out a cube.
Packing cubes.action: One cube per kind of thing, not per outfit. Keep one empty at the start and let it become the laundry cube.

Golden hour.title: Golden hour
Golden hour.sub: The hour that does the work for you
Golden hour.explain: Let's say your photos look flat and you've blamed the camera. Midday sun comes straight down, so it fills every shadow, and shadows are what make things look solid. Late light comes in low and sideways. It rakes across whatever you point at, so you get long shadows and texture. Depth you didn't have to add. Same phone, same spot. Different hour.
Golden hour.action: Shoot the hour after sunrise or the hour before sunset, and put the sun to one side of your subject rather than behind you.

Progressive overload.title: Progressive overload
Progressive overload.sub: A little more than last week
Progressive overload.explain: Let's say you've been going to the gym for months, you never miss a session, and you look exactly the same. You've been lifting the same weight the whole time. Your body only builds what it keeps being asked for. Ask for the same thing every week and it has no reason to change. Ask for slightly more, one extra rep or the smallest plate on the bar, and it has to adapt. Small, boring, every week. That is the whole method.
Progressive overload.action: Write down what you lifted. Next session add one rep, or the smallest weight you own. If you can't, keep it and try again next week.

The emergency fund.title: The emergency fund
The emergency fund.sub: The money you hope to waste
The emergency fund.explain: Let's say the car dies on a Tuesday and it's eight hundred to fix. It goes on a card, and now you're paying for that Tuesday for the next year. The fix isn't earning more. It's a boring pile of cash you never touch, three months of what it costs you to live, in its own account. When the bad Tuesday comes, it's just an errand. It isn't an investment. It's what stops one bad week becoming a bad year.
The emergency fund.action: Add up one month of what you actually spend. Open a separate account, set a small automatic transfer, and don't link it to a card.

Spaced repetition.title: Spaced repetition
Spaced repetition.explain: Let's say you sit down and learn twenty new words. You feel great about it. A week later you can remember four, and the other sixteen cost you an evening. A word gets stronger when you pull it back just as it's about to slip. Too soon and you learn nothing, because it was still there. Too late and it's gone. So the gaps start small and get wider: tomorrow, a few days, a week, three weeks. You don't need more hours. You need better timing.
Spaced repetition.action: Take five new words. See them tomorrow, in three days, in a week, in three weeks. Anything you miss goes back to the start of the ladder.

The fork.title: The fork
The fork.explain: Let's say you lose a piece most games and you never see it coming. It usually isn't a deep trap. It's one piece attacking two of yours at once. The knight is the worst for this, because it jumps and nothing blocks it. Once it hits your king and something valuable on the same move, the check has to be answered first, and whatever else it was hitting is gone next move. You don't have to be clever. You just have to see it first.
The fork.action: Before every move, look for one square where a knight would hit two things. Do it for your knights, then theirs.

Circuit breaker.title: Circuit breaker
Circuit breaker.sub: Stop calling the thing that's down
Circuit breaker.explain: Let's say your app asks another service for something, maybe a payment check. One morning it's down, and your whole app goes slow, including the parts that don't use it. Every request sits there waiting to time out. A breaker counts the failures, and after a few in a row it stops calling and answers straight away with whatever you chose to say instead. Now and then it tries one real call. One thing broke. Not everything.
Circuit breaker.action: Put a circuit breaker around my calls to this service. Open it after a few failures, return a fallback right away, and retry one call now and then.
